posts.headline: Turn toward the small bids
posts.text:
Most connection in a relationship doesn't happen on date night. It happens in tiny moments: "Look at that bird," a sigh in the kitchen, a hand on your shoulder.

Relationship researchers John and Julie Gottman call these "bids." Couples who stay close tend to notice them and turn toward them, even with a quick "Huh, cool" or a look up from the phone.

This week, try catching one or two bids you'd usually miss. Small turns add up.

posts.headline: Holidays and old stress
posts.text:
If the holidays make you feel tense, short-tempered or far away from yourself, you're not alone.

Family gatherings can bring back old roles and old memories, sometimes before you even notice it happening.

It helps to plan ahead: decide how long you'll stay, have a way to step outside for a few minutes, and agree on a signal with your partner if you need to leave early. Planning isn't avoiding. It's taking care of yourself.

posts.headline: The gentle start-up
posts.text:
How a hard conversation starts often decides how it ends.

A harsh start ("You never help with anything") usually gets defense back. A gentler start sounds more like: "I'm feeling stretched thin this week. Could you take the dishes tonight?"

It has three parts: how you feel, about what situation, and what you need. It feels awkward at first. That's normal.

posts.headline: What a 15-minute consult is for
posts.text:
A free consult isn't a sales call and it isn't therapy yet. It's a chance to see if we're a good fit.

You can ask how I work, what sessions look like, fees and scheduling. I'll ask a little about what's bringing you in, so I can tell you honestly whether I'm the right person or point you to someone who is.

You can book one at stonesrivertherapy.com/book or call or text (615) 200-0063.

posts.headline: Your nervous system isn't broken
posts.text:
After something hard happens, the body can stay on alert long after the danger is over. Jumpiness, trouble sleeping, snapping at people you love, or feeling numb can all be signs of that.

That isn't weakness. It's a nervous system doing its job a little too well.

Therapy for trauma often starts with steadiness first: learning what helps your body settle, before working with harder memories.

posts.headline: Thanksgiving with a side of tension
posts.text:
A few things that help couples get through a tense family gathering:

- Agree on arrival and leave times before you go
- Pick one topic you'll both steer away from
- Check in with each other halfway through, even just "You okay?"
- Debrief on the drive home with curiosity, not blame

You're on the same team, even when the room doesn't feel like it.

posts.headline: Repair is a skill
posts.text:
Every couple argues. What matters most is whether you can repair.

A repair can be small: "Can we start over?" "I'm getting too heated, give me a minute." "I see your point on that part."

Repairs work better when both people are willing to accept them. If your partner reaches out mid-fight, try to meet them halfway, even if you're still upset.

posts.headline: Grounding for hard moments
posts.text:
When you feel flooded or far away, a simple grounding exercise can help bring you back to the present:

Name 5 things you can see, 4 you can feel, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, and 1 you can taste.

It won't fix everything, but it can give your body a moment to settle. If you're ever in crisis, call or text 988, any time.

posts.headline: Therapy by video in Tennessee
posts.text:
Telehealth sessions work well for a lot of people: no drive, no waiting room, and you're in a space that already feels familiar.

A few tips: find a private spot where you won't be overheard, use headphones if you can, and give yourself 5 quiet minutes before and after.

Video sessions are available for adults who are physically in Tennessee at the time of the session.

posts.headline: Take a break before you flood
posts.text:
When an argument gets heated, your heart rate climbs and it gets hard to think clearly. Researchers call it flooding.

If that happens, it's okay to take a break. Say when you'll come back ("Give me 20 minutes and let's try again"), then do something calming, not something that keeps the argument going in your head.

The coming back part is what makes it a break and not a walkout.

posts.headline: December is a lot
posts.text:
Between money, travel, family and the pressure to feel merry, December can be one of the hardest months of the year.

It's okay if this season feels heavy. It's okay to keep traditions small, say no to some invitations, or make new plans that fit the life you have now.

Be as kind to yourself as you'd be to a friend having the same month.

posts.headline: What EMDR is, in plain words
posts.text:
EMDR stands for Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing. It's a well-researched therapy for trauma.

In EMDR, you focus briefly on part of a hard memory while doing something side-to-side, like following a light with your eyes or gentle tapping. Over time, many people find the memory feels less sharp and the beliefs tied to it ("It was my fault," "I'm not safe") start to loosen.

It starts with preparation and coping skills first. You set the pace.

posts.headline: Ask open-ended questions
posts.text:
After years together, it's easy to stop asking real questions. "How was your day?" gets "Fine."

Try questions that can't be answered in one word:
- What's been on your mind lately?
- What's something you're looking forward to?
- What's one thing I could do this week that would help?

Then listen like you're getting to know them. In a way, you are.

posts.headline: When the holidays bring up grief
posts.text:
Holidays can make an empty chair feel even emptier, whether you've lost a person, a relationship, or the way things used to be.

Some people find it helps to name the loss out loud, set a place or light a candle, or plan one quiet moment for themselves in a busy day.

There's no right way to grieve during the holidays. Gentle is enough.

posts.headline: Couples therapy isn't only for crisis
posts.text:
Many couples wait years after problems start before they reach out for help.

You don't have to wait for things to fall apart. Couples therapy can help when you keep having the same fight, feel more like roommates, or are heading into a big change like a move, a new baby or retirement.

Starting early is usually easier, not harder.

posts.headline: Sleep and stress
posts.text:
Stress and sleep feed each other. When one goes, the other often follows.

A few basics that help: keep a steady wake-up time, put the phone down a little before bed, and if your mind races, write the worries on paper so they're out of your head for the night.

If trouble sleeping goes on for weeks, it's worth talking to your doctor.

posts.headline: The roommate feeling
posts.text:
Busy schedules, kids, work, and screens can slowly turn partners into roommates who run a household together.

It's common, and it can change. Small rituals help: a 10-minute check-in after work, a weekly walk, a real goodbye kiss in the morning.

Connection usually comes back through small, steady habits more than big gestures.

posts.headline: Boundaries over the holidays
posts.text:
A boundary isn't a punishment. It's a clear statement of what you will and won't do.

"We'll be there from 2 to 5." "I'm not going to talk about my weight." "If the drinking starts, we're heading home."

You can say it kindly and still mean it. Other people's reactions aren't yours to manage.

posts.headline: New year, gentler goals
posts.text:
If you're setting goals for the new year, consider making them kinder and smaller.

"Fix my marriage" is a lot. "Have one real conversation a week" is doable. "Stop being anxious" is hard. "Notice when I'm tense and take three slow breaths" is a place to start.

Small steps you'll actually take beat big ones that make you feel like you failed.

posts.headline: Trust is rebuilt in small pieces
posts.text:
After a breach of trust, many couples hope for one big conversation that fixes everything. Trust usually doesn't work that way.

It's rebuilt through small things done again and again: being where you said you'd be, answering questions honestly, following through.

It takes time, and it takes both people. Couples therapy can give that work some structure and a safe place to have the hard talks.

posts.headline: What the first session looks like
posts.text:
Wondering what actually happens in a first therapy session?

Mostly, we get to know each other. I'll ask what's bringing you in, a little about your history, and what you'd like to be different. You can ask me anything too.

You don't have to share everything at once. We go at a pace that feels okay to you.

posts.headline: Know your stress signals
posts.text:
Most of us have early signs that stress is building: a tight jaw, a short temper, scrolling for hours, not wanting to talk.

If you know your early signals, you can step in sooner, before you're at a 10.

It also helps to tell your partner what your signals look like, so they know what's going on when they see them.

posts.headline: Fondness and admiration
posts.text:
Couples who stay close keep noticing what they like about each other, even during hard seasons.

Try this: once a day this week, tell your partner one specific thing you appreciated. "Thanks for getting up with the dog." "You were really patient with your mom today."

It sounds simple. It's one of the strongest habits a couple can build.

posts.headline: Triggers, explained
posts.text:
A trigger is something in the present that sets off a strong reaction tied to the past: a tone of voice, a smell, a time of year, a certain kind of argument.

Noticing a trigger is a skill. So is pausing to ask, "Is this about right now, or is something older showing up?"

If you're ever in crisis, call or text 988 for support any time.

posts.headline: Winter blues are real
posts.text:
Shorter days and less sunlight can drag a lot of people's mood and energy down in January and February.

Getting outside in daylight, moving your body, and keeping plans with people you like can all help.

If low mood sticks around for weeks or gets in the way of daily life, talk with your doctor or a therapist. You don't have to wait it out alone.

posts.headline: Fight about the problem, not each other
posts.text:
In an argument, try to keep the problem as the thing you're both facing, not each other.

"We keep running late in the morning, what could make it easier?" lands very differently from "You always make us late."

Same topic. One invites teamwork, the other invites a defense.

posts.headline: Couples intensives
posts.text:
Some couples don't want to wait weeks between sessions. An intensive is a longer session, about 3 hours, that gives you room to go deeper in one sitting.

Intensives can help when you're at a turning point, after a breach of trust, or when schedules make weekly sessions hard.

Details and fees are posted at stonesrivertherapy.com/intensives.

posts.headline: It's okay to start therapy alone
posts.text:
Sometimes one partner is ready for therapy and the other isn't yet.

You can still start on your own. Understanding your own patterns, what you need, and how you respond under stress can change how the whole relationship feels.

A free 15-minute consult is a low-pressure way to see if it's a fit: stonesrivertherapy.com/book

posts.headline: Self-compassion after trauma
posts.text:
Many people who've been through trauma are much harder on themselves than they'd ever be on someone else.

Try this: when you notice harsh self-talk, ask, "What would I say to a friend who went through this?" Then try saying it to yourself.

It can feel strange at first. Kindness toward yourself is a skill, and it can be practiced.

posts.headline: Valentine's Day pressure
posts.text:
Valentine's Day can feel like a test: big plans, the perfect gift, posting about it.

What tends to matter more is the everyday stuff: feeling noticed, feeling like a team, laughing together.

If you'd like to do something, keep it simple and personal. A note about why you're glad you're together can mean more than an expensive dinner.

posts.headline: Talking about money as a couple
posts.text:
Money is one of the most common things couples fight about, often because it carries big feelings: safety, fairness, freedom, family history.

Try a calm, scheduled money talk instead of fighting about it in the moment. Start with what money meant in each of your families growing up. It usually explains a lot.

posts.headline: Why I see adults only
posts.text:
My practice is for adults 18 and up: couples and individuals.

If you're looking for help for a child or teen, your pediatrician or school counselor can be a good place to ask for referrals.

If you're an adult wondering whether therapy could help, a free 15-minute consult is a good first step.

posts.headline: Make a plan for hard days
posts.text:
On a good day, write down what helps you on a hard day: people to call, places to go, things that calm you down, reasons to keep going.

Keep it somewhere easy to find, like your phone notes.

On a hard day it's tough to think clearly, so your good-day self can help your hard-day self. And if you're in crisis, call or text 988, any time, day or night.

posts.headline: Accepting influence
posts.text:
In strong relationships, both partners let the other one influence them. That doesn't mean giving in on everything. It means really considering your partner's point of view and finding the part you can say yes to.

"That's a fair point, let's try it your way this time."

When both people feel heard, decisions get easier.

posts.headline: Fees, posted up front
posts.text:
Therapy shouldn't come with surprise costs. Session fees, intensives and cancellation terms are posted at stonesrivertherapy.com/fees.

I'm private pay, and I can provide a superbill you can submit to your insurance for possible out-of-network reimbursement. You'll also get a written Good Faith Estimate before your first session.

posts.headline: Rituals of connection
posts.text:
A ritual of connection is something small you do together on purpose, again and again.

Coffee together before the house wakes up. A walk after dinner. Saying goodnight without screens. A Sunday check-in about the week ahead.

They give a relationship something steady to come back to when life gets busy.

posts.headline: Healing isn't a straight line
posts.text:
Progress in therapy often looks like two steps forward, one step back. A hard week doesn't erase the work you've done.

It can help to look back over months, not days. Are you recovering faster after a rough moment? Noticing your patterns sooner?

That counts. That's healing.

posts.headline: An apology that lands
posts.text:
A real apology is short and doesn't come with a "but."

It names what happened, owns your part, and shows you understand how it affected the other person: "I snapped at you in front of your sister. That was embarrassing for you, and I'm sorry."

Then give it time. The other person may need a moment before they're ready to move on.

posts.headline: Starting therapy this year
posts.text:
If you've been thinking about therapy for a while, here's what getting started looks like:

1. Book a free 15-minute consult at stonesrivertherapy.com/book
2. We talk about what's bringing you in and whether we're a fit
3. If so, you'll get paperwork and a Good Faith Estimate before your first session

In person in Murfreesboro or by video anywhere in Tennessee.
